h1: Lawn fertilization in Longview & East Texas
lede: Soil-tested feeding, core aeration and a fall winterizer, timed to when East Texas grass can actually use it. Visits start from about $190.
answer: Yard Dog Landscapes is a family-owned company in Longview, TX, founded in 2017 and rated 5.0 stars across 111 Google reviews. We fertilize bermuda, St. Augustine and Zoysia lawns on a schedule built for East Texas: a soil test first, slow-release feedings in late April, early July and early September, and a potassium-heavy winterizer in October. We also core aerate compacted lawns. Visits start from about $190, depending on lawn size and how many rounds it needs. Text (903) 522-5291.
overview: Fertilization isn't about putting down more. It's about putting it down the week the grass can use it. We start with a soil test, then build a feeding schedule around your grass type and the East Texas season, not the back of a bag written for somewhere up north.

A full program is four visits. Slow-release nitrogen goes down in late April once nights hold above 60 degrees. A lighter, summer-safe feeding follows in early July so the lawn doesn't run on empty through August. The last real nitrogen goes down in early September to push roots before dormancy, and a low-nitrogen, potassium-heavy winterizer goes down in October for cold hardiness. If the test shows low pH, which is common here, we correct it with lime. Core aeration fits in late summer on compacted lawns.

timing: The first feeding goes down around April 25, once overnight lows hold above 60 and the grass is fully awake. Feed in March and most of it washes out with the next rain, because bermuda and St. Augustine are still half-dormant and can't pull it in. The last nitrogen goes down in the first two weeks of September, four to six weeks ahead of Longview's mid-November first freeze.

east_texas.title: The bag on the shelf was written for somebody else's lawn
text: Big-box stores stack fertilizer out front the first week it hits 60 degrees, and they stack winterizer by the door in October. Both schedules were written for cool-season lawns up north. Soil in Gregg and Harrison counties doesn't reach 65 degrees until mid-April, and a heavy shot of nitrogen in mid-October pushes soft growth right before frost burns it off.

On St. Augustine, late nitrogen is worse than wasted. Large patch wakes up when nights drop into the 60s and the grass stays damp overnight, which is October here, and late feeding fuels it. That is why our last real nitrogen goes down in early September and October is a potassium month. Years of pine needles and acidic rain also push most East Texas soil a little low on pH, so we test and add lime when it's needed.

faq.q: When should I fertilize my lawn in East Texas?
faq.a: The spring window opens around April 25, once nights hold above 60 degrees, and runs through May. After that, keep the tank from running dry with a lighter feeding in early July and a fall feeding in early September. Skip March, when the grass is still half-dormant, and skip heavy nitrogen in October, when it only pushes growth the frost will burn off.

faq.q: Does your fertilization program include weed control?
faq.a: No. We are not a spray outfit, and we don't apply weed, insect or disease products of any kind. Our program is fertilizer, soil testing, lime when the test calls for it, core aeration and the fall winterizer. If you want a lawn sprayed, that is a job for a pest control company. What we do is keep the grass itself fed and well rooted.

Yes. We core aerate, which pulls plugs out of the ground instead of poking holes, because a spike aerator just shoves clay sideways and packs it tighter. The window here is late August through mid-September, while the grass can still heal the holes. The lawn should be watered the day before so the tines don't skip on dry clay, and the plugs stay where they fall.

faq.q: Do bermuda and St. Augustine need a winterizer?
faq.a: Not the high-nitrogen kind sold for cool-season lawns. Our grasses slow down in fall instead of growing into December, so late nitrogen just pushes soft growth the frost burns off, and on St. Augustine it can feed large patch. What helps is a low-nitrogen, potassium-heavy feeding in October for rooting and cold hardiness, if the soil test says the lawn needs it.
